lede: Formula 1 rewrote its rulebook for 2026, with engines that take half their power from the battery, wings that open on the straights and smaller, lighter cars, and Mercedes read it best. Kimi Antonelli clinched the drivers' title in Mexico City at 20, the youngest champion in the sport's history, and a week later fourth and fifth places in a wet São Paulo race sealed Mercedes' first constructors' title since 2021. Lando Norris won that race in an upgraded McLaren, his third win of the year, while Max Verstappen climbed from 21st to second. With three rounds left, the fight is for second place: Verstappen has 279 points, 17 ahead of George Russell and 18 ahead of Lewis Hamilton. The newcomers, Audi (which took over Sauber) and Cadillac, have found it hard going, and war in the Middle East wiped out April's races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia; Bahrain's was run in Malaysia instead.

rounds.headline: Russell opens the new era with a Mercedes one-two

Battery management on Melbourne's long straights dominated the first race of the new rules, and five cars failed to finish. [1][2][3]

rounds.report: Hamilton put Ferrari on pole for the first time this year, but the race turned at Turn 4 on the opening lap. Leclerc went around the outside of his teammate, both cars ran off the track, and Leclerc came out in front while Hamilton's poor exit let Verstappen through. Leclerc was given a five-second penalty, and Russell ten seconds for spinning Hadjar at Turn 6. [1][2][3] Verstappen had started on mediums; when he switched to softs on lap 27, the same lap as Leclerc's stop, he took the lead. Antonelli stayed out longer and pitted just before Bottas crashed heavily at Turn 1 with a front-left suspension failure. The safety car became a red flag for barrier repairs, and every driver chose softs for the run to the flag. [1][2][4] At the restart Antonelli passed Leclerc for third. A late safety car for Lindblad's crash after contact with Piastri left an eight-lap sprint, and Verstappen held Hamilton off by 0.8 seconds. Third place made Antonelli champion at 20 with four rounds to spare, the youngest in F1 history and Italy's first since Alberto Ascari in 1953. [1][3]

rounds.report: Rain shaped the weekend. Qualifying was wet and red-flagged, and Norris took pole in the upgraded McLaren. Power-unit penalties then reshaped the grid: Hamilton dropped 75 places to 20th, Verstappen and Pérez 30 places each, Leclerc, Lindblad and Bortoleto ten each and Russell five, which put Antonelli and Lawson behind Norris on the grid. [4][5] The race started on intermediates and Norris got away poorly, falling to third while Antonelli built a lead of more than eight seconds. Norris passed Lawson on lap 6. Hamilton was first onto slicks at the end of lap 14, Norris followed two laps later and Antonelli a lap after that, rejoining barely ahead. Short of tyre temperature, Antonelli spun at Turn 1 on lap 20 and handed Norris the lead, and both Red Bulls soon passed him. [1][2] Verstappen carved through from 21st, with Hadjar told to let him by on lap 38. When the rain came back the field returned to intermediates with about ten laps left, and Norris pulled clear to win by 14.6 seconds, with Hadjar completing a Red Bull double podium. [1][2][3] Fourth for Russell, despite a spin at the pit exit, and fifth for Antonelli were enough for Mercedes to seal its ninth constructors' title, its first since 2021, with three rounds to go. [1][3]

storylines.body: Kimi Antonelli won his first Grand Prix in China as a teenager, took the championship lead in Japan as the youngest leader in F1 history, and never gave it up. Even a mid-season wobble (a retirement in Barcelona and a 15th at Silverstone) did not cost him the lead, and wins from 19th at Monza and in Madrid put him out of reach of most rivals. [1][2][3] Victory in Austin left him 123 points clear, and third place in Mexico City, where he passed Leclerc at the red-flag restart, settled it with four rounds left. At 20 he beats Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest champion by about three years, and he is Italy's first title winner since Alberto Ascari in 1953. [5][6]

storylines.title: Mercedes mastered the 2026 reset
storylines.body: The all-new rules (no MGU-H, a near 50-50 split between combustion and electric power, sustainable fuel, smaller cars and active aero in place of DRS) produced a clear early pecking order with Mercedes on top. The works team won the first six races and 12 of the first 20. Mercedes-powered McLaren is the only other team to win with that engine, while Red Bull's in-house Ford-backed unit took until October to win. Ferrari and its customers have won only twice. [1][2][3] Fourth and fifth places in São Paulo gave Mercedes the constructors' title with three rounds left, its ninth and its first since the eight straight it won from 2014 to 2021, which draws it level with Williams for third on the all-time list. [4][5]

storylines.title: Energy management row and the FIA's in-season fixes
storylines.body: From Melbourne onward, drivers had to lift and coast to recharge batteries that supply about half the car's power, and some circuits exposed that badly. At Suzuka, Bearman suffered a 50G crash after running into a large speed difference with a car that was harvesting energy, and drivers including Alonso criticised the rules openly. The FIA met the power unit makers four times in April and, before Miami, raised the 'super clipping' limit to 350kW and cut the qualifying harvest allowance from 8MJ to 7MJ. Battery deployment still decided battles as late as Monza. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.title: War redraws the calendar
storylines.body: Escalating conflict involving Iran forced the cancellation of April's Bahrain and Saudi Arabian rounds, announced around the Chinese GP, and the calendar briefly fell to 22 races. In late July, F1 and the FIA agreed to run the Bahrain GP at Sepang in Malaysia on 4 October, keeping Bahrain as promoter and bringing the season back to 23 rounds. Saudi Arabia was never reinstated. The Qatar and Abu Dhabi finale stayed in doubt for months, with Imola as a fallback, until Domenicali confirmed both in early October subject to security assurances. A mid-October deadline then passed with no change. [1][2][3][4]

storylines.body: Esteban Ocon's final season at Haas has turned sour. The team told him before Baku that he would not be retained, and on 15 October signed Ferrari junior and F2 leader Rafael Câmara for 2027. [1][2] In Mexico City, after Ocon protested over the radio when his Friday run plan was changed, Haas replaced him for the rest of the weekend with reserve Ryo Hirakawa. Team principal Ayao Komatsu said Ocon was not ill but gave no reason. [2] Hirakawa, 32, a Le Mans winner and two-time world endurance champion with Toyota, scored a point in tenth on debut. [3] On 3 November Haas confirmed Ocon would not race for it again and brought Câmara's debut forward to São Paulo, his home race. [5] He qualified in the top 13 in the wet but finished 20th, two laps down, after several slides. [6]

storylines.title: Hamilton's breakthrough and Ferrari's near-misses
storylines.body: Hamilton took his first Grand Prix podium for Ferrari in China and his first win for the team in Barcelona, where an aggressive three-stop strategy and a well-timed virtual safety car beat Mercedes. Leclerc added victory at Silverstone, and Ferrari is a solid second in the constructors' table. Costly errors have held them back, though: Hamilton's ignored pit call in Singapore cost a podium, and pit-lane and collision penalties hurt him in Hungary and Belgium. [1][2][3] Mexico City summed up the year: Hamilton took Ferrari's first pole of 2026, Leclerc forced him wide at Turn 4 on lap 1 to take the lead, and Verstappen slipped past both to win. Hamilton finished second and said the team needed serious talks behind the scenes. [4][5] In São Paulo Hamilton took a 75-place grid penalty for a second set of new power-unit parts and Leclerc a ten-place one; they finished ninth and eighth, and Fred Vasseur said the team could not get its tyres into the right window. [6][7]

storylines.title: Verstappen and Red Bull-Ford's autumn revival
storylines.body: Red Bull's first season with its own Ford-backed power unit started roughly: Verstappen crashed in Melbourne qualifying, retired in China, stalled and retired in Monaco, and crashed out at both Silverstone and Zandvoort. Steady podiums from Austria onward came before a breakthrough in October, with wins in the rain at Sepang and a clean sweep in Singapore on his 250th start. Hadjar has backed him up with podiums in Monaco and Baku, and Red Bull is third in the constructors' table. [1][2][3][4] Verstappen then won from fifth on the grid in Mexico City, starting on mediums and holding off Hamilton at the final restart, and moved up to second in the championship. [5][6] In São Paulo a 30-place penalty for new power-unit parts put Verstappen 21st on the grid; he finished second, with Hadjar third after letting him through on lap 38. [8][7]

storylines.title: Hard landings for Cadillac, Audi and Aston Martin-Honda
storylines.body: New entrant Cadillac, running Ferrari engines with veterans Perez and Bottas, is the only team without a point after 19 rounds, and both cars have been regular retirements. Audi's first season as a works team has brought 23 points and eighth place. Aston Martin's new partnership with Honda has delivered just seven points, and Stroll's car has stopped on track often enough to trigger neutralisations in China, Monza, Madrid and Singapore. Midfield reports still describe the car as short on power. [1][2][3][4] Mexico City was harsh on both: Alonso and Stroll retired in the first seven laps, and Bottas crashed at Turn 1 after a front-left suspension failure, which led to a red flag. [5][6] São Paulo brought more of the same: Bottas could not start because a wheel nut stuck on the grid, Stroll retired with a battery problem, and Cadillac is still without a point after 20 rounds. [7]

title.text: Both titles are settled. Antonelli became drivers' champion in Mexico City and has 390 points with nine wins. In São Paulo Mercedes moved to 652 points against Ferrari's 510; a team can score at most 43 points in a weekend, so with three rounds left Ferrari could gain no more than 129 of the 142-point gap, and Mercedes is constructors' champion. [1][2][3] Three rounds remain (Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi), none of them sprints, so a driver can add at most 75 points (25 for a win; there is no fastest-lap point). Second place is open: Verstappen (279) leads Russell (262) by 17 points, Hamilton (261) by 18, Leclerc (249) by 30 and Norris (246) by 33, while Piastri (152) can no longer reach him. In the constructors' table Ferrari (510) leads Red Bull (415) by 95 points and McLaren (398) by 112, so both can still mathematically take second. [2]

calendar: The 2026 season was announced with 24 rounds. Bahrain and Saudi Arabia (originally April) were cancelled because of the Middle East conflict. On 26 July 2026 F1 brought the Bahrain Grand Prix back, staged at Sepang, Malaysia, on 2-4 October, which makes 23 rounds. Saudi Arabia was not replaced. As of late July and August 2026, F1 said Qatar and Abu Dhabi were confirmed and sold out, with a European finale (Imola reported) kept as a contingency. The six Sprint weekends are China, Miami, Canada, Britain, Netherlands and Singapore. Rounds 1-20 have been run; the next race is Las Vegas, with the race on the Saturday night of 21 November local time. [1][2][3][4][5][6]
